title: Kimmel's ABC show won't air interview with Democrat because of Trump FCC threats
gist: Jimmy Kimmel moved an interview with Texas Senate candidate James Talarico to YouTube rather than broadcast it, citing FCC threats to the licenses of ABC affiliates, after Chairman Brendan Carr's FCC ordered early license review of all eight ABC-owned stations and opened a proceeding on whether The View still qualifies for the equal-time exemption. Disney sued the FCC in August on First Amendment grounds, the FCC has asked a court to dismiss, and watchdogs fear a settlement that limits ABC station content ahead of the midterms.

themes.theme: Regulatory pressure reshaping broadcast editorial decisions

insights.claim: Jimmy Kimmel moved his interview with Texas state representative and Senate candidate James Talarico to the Jimmy Kimmel Live YouTube channel instead of broadcast television specifically to avoid creating FCC license trouble for ABC affiliates, especially those in Texas.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Political content is migrating from licensed broadcast to unlicensed platforms under regulatory pressure, structurally shifting audience and ad value toward YouTube.
insights.locator: ABC’s Jimmy Kimmel said he will be interviewing

insights.claim: Kimmel says he interviewed candidates from Hillary Clinton to Ted Cruz to Donald Trump across more than 20 years of the show with no problem, and that Trump himself was eager to return for a second interview before becoming the 2016 nominee.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Establishes that the practice was uncontroversial for two decades, framing the change as regulatory rather than a shift in industry norms.
insights.quote: I’ve been interviewing Americans who are running for office with no problem at all, just like Letterman did, Leno did, Arsenio, et cetera
insights.locator: “I’ll be interviewing James Talarico tomorrow night

insights.claim: Kimmel says the FCC has threatened him, his show, his network ABC, its affiliates and local stations based on simple traditional editorial decisions and guest bookings the commission appears to dislike.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: The claimed threat runs down to the affiliate level, meaning the chilling effect reaches independently owned station groups, not just Disney.
insights.quote: his FCC has threatened me, threatened our show, threatened our network, ABC, our affiliates, our local stations, based on simple, traditional editorial decisions, guest bookings it would seem they don’t like.

insights.claim: Stephen Colbert faced the same dynamic in February when CBS blocked him from interviewing Talarico on air and he posted it to YouTube, with CBS denying a prohibition but saying it gave legal guidance that broadcast could trigger equal-time obligations for two other candidates.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: The pattern spans at least two major networks, indicating an industry-wide compliance posture rather than a single company's dispute.
insights.locator: An interview with Talarico was also at the center

insights.claim: The Carr FCC ordered an early license review for all eight TV stations owned by ABC in April, one day after Trump and the first lady called on ABC to fire Kimmel over a joke, with the FCC framing the review as an investigation of ABC's DEI practices under anti-discrimination rules.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: License review is the concrete enforcement lever; its timing relative to presidential comments is the fact pattern Disney is litigating.

insights.claim: Disney briefly suspended Kimmel last year after FCC Chairman Brendan Carr threatened to revoke the licenses of ABC stations for news distortion if they continued airing the show.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: A license threat has already produced a corporate content concession once, which is why markets should treat further threats as likely to move programming.
insights.locator: But as Kimmel said, “something has changed.”

insights.claim: The FCC opened a proceeding in May 2026 examining whether ABC's The View should remain exempt from the equal-time rule as a bona fide news interview program, and The View has aired no interviews with political candidates since.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: An open proceeding alone, with no adverse ruling, was sufficient to end a programming practice, demonstrating how process functions as the penalty.
insights.locator: The Carr FCC also started investigating ABC’s The View

insights.claim: Until Carr took over, the FCC historically treated interview talk shows as exempt from the equal-time rule, but in January the Carr FCC ordered broadcast stations to comply with equal time for late-night and daytime talk shows motivated by partisan purposes while making no similar move against predominantly conservative talk radio.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Asymmetric application across formats is the core of the viewpoint-discrimination argument and the strongest predictor of how courts may rule.
insights.locator: Until Carr took over at the FCC

insights.claim: Disney sued the FCC in August alleging First Amendment violations and stating that ABC must now evaluate any invitation to a political candidate for whether it might later be cited as a basis for non-renewal in the stations' impending license renewal proceedings.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Disney has put the chilling effect on the record in a filing, which both preserves its legal claim and documents a real constraint on its programming.
insights.quote: ABC must now evaluate any invitation to a political candidate for its potential consequences, including whether it might later be cited by the Commission as a basis for non-renewal
insights.locator: Disney sued the FCC in August

insights.claim: The FCC urged a court last week to dismiss Disney's lawsuit and let it continue a proceeding that could end in the nonrenewal of broadcast licenses held by ABC-owned stations.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Nonrenewal of owned-and-operated station licenses is a tangible asset-impairment scenario for Disney, not just a reputational fight.
insights.locator: Disney’s legal fight against the FCC is ongoing

insights.claim: Watchdog groups told the court they fear Disney will settle with the FCC in a way that limits the content provided by ABC stations.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: The likely resolution is a negotiated content constraint rather than a precedent-setting ruling, which preserves the leverage for future administrations.

insights.claim: Disney argues the campaign against ABC will be particularly damaging during the months before the midterm election, tying the regulatory dispute directly to election-period political coverage.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Election timing raises the stakes and the odds of expedited judicial intervention, making the coming weeks the decision window.
insights.locator: Disney said the Trump administration’s campaign of censorship

insights.claim: FCC Commissioner Anna Gomez, the commission's only Democrat, said the agency has no lawful authority to threaten broadcast licenses over guest bookings or editorial decisions and that pressuring broadcasters into self-censorship undermines press freedom and the public's right to hear from candidates.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: A sitting commissioner disputing the agency's own authority strengthens the record for judicial review and signals internal division at the FCC.
insights.quote: no host, local affiliate, or network should have to weigh federal retaliation before booking a guest for a newsworthy interview
insights.locator: “Jimmy Kimmel’s decision to keep his interview
